title: Can Non-Alcoholic Beer Give You a Hangover? NA Beer and Wine
excerpt: Can non-alcoholic beer give you a hangover? Why 0.5% and 0.0% drinks can't cause a true hangover, the real reasons you may still feel rough, and what NA wine and Guinness 0.0 do.
metaDescription: Can non-alcoholic beer or wine give you a hangover? Why 0.5% beer can't cause a true one, and the real reasons you may still feel rough the next day.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** non-alcoholic beer can't give you a true hangover, but it can leave you feeling rough the next morning. A real hangover is driven mostly by alcohol itself: the toxic by-product your liver makes from it, broken sleep, inflammation, and lost fluids. A 0.5% beer contains so little alcohol that your body clears it about as fast as you drink it, so none of that machinery really switches on. What *can* happen is a headache, a bloated stomach, poor sleep, or a foggy morning caused by other things: carbonation, sugar, a late night, histamine or gluten sensitivity, the food you ate, or simply expecting to feel hungover. The same is true for non-alcoholic wine and for drinks like Guinness 0.0.

**The quick rules:** If you drank only 0.0% or 0.5% drinks and feel awful, the cause is almost certainly something other than alcohol, so look at sleep, food, sugar, and sensitivities. If you mixed NA beers with regular drinks, the hangover is coming from the regular drinks. And if you need to avoid alcohol completely for a medical, legal, or personal reason, choose products labeled 0.0% and read the fine print.

> **This is general information, not medical advice.** **When to see a doctor:** Most "NA beer hangovers" are mild and gone by lunchtime. Get medical help if you have a sudden, severe headache (the worst of your life), a headache with fever, stiff neck, confusion, weakness, or vision changes, or vomiting you can't keep fluids down through. **Call 911 or go to the emergency room** if you notice hives with swelling of the lips, tongue, or throat, or trouble breathing after a drink, which can signal an allergic reaction. If you take **disulfiram (Antabuse), metronidazole, or an MAOI antidepressant**, or you are pregnant, have liver disease, or have been told to avoid all alcohol, talk to your doctor before drinking any "non-alcoholic" beer or wine, because even trace alcohol or the natural compounds in fermented drinks can matter for you. Flushing, pounding heart, and vomiting after an NA beer while on disulfiram is a reason to get care right away.

## Can Non-Alcoholic Beer Give You a Hangover?

Not in the usual sense. To see why, it helps to know what a hangover actually is.

When you drink regular alcohol, your liver breaks ethanol down into **acetaldehyde**, a toxic compound that causes nausea, flushing, and headache, and then clears it further. Alcohol also suppresses a hormone that helps you hold onto water, so you lose more fluid. It fragments your sleep, especially the second half of the night. It irritates the stomach lining, and it triggers a low-grade inflammatory response that many researchers think is central to how bad you feel the next day. Our guide to [hangover symptoms](/never-hungover/hangover-symptoms) walks through each of these in more detail.

Every one of those effects depends on the dose of alcohol. Here is roughly how much alcohol is in a typical non-alcoholic beer:

| Drink | Alcohol by volume | Approximate alcohol in a 12 oz (355 ml) serving |
|---|---|---|
| Regular beer | about 5% | about 14 g (one US standard drink) |
| Light beer | about 4.2% | about 12 g |
| "Non-alcoholic" beer | up to 0.5% | up to about 1.4 g |
| "Alcohol-free" or 0.0% beer | under 0.05% in most markets | a trace |

A healthy adult clears roughly one standard drink (about 14 g of alcohol) per hour, although this varies from person to person. A 0.5% beer delivers about a tenth of that. So even if you sip several over an evening, your liver is clearing the alcohol about as fast as it arrives, and your blood alcohol stays near zero. Research testing people who drank large volumes of non-alcoholic beer has generally found blood alcohol levels that were tiny or undetectable, far below anything that would cause intoxication.

No meaningful alcohol means no real acetaldehyde load, no alcohol-driven fluid loss, and no alcohol-driven sleep disruption. That is why a true hangover from NA beer alone is very unlikely. For the full breakdown of what's in the can, see our explainer on [whether non-alcoholic beer has alcohol](/never-hungover/does-non-alcoholic-beer-have-alcohol).

### "Then why do I feel hungover?"

Plenty of people do wake up feeling off after a night of NA beers. That feeling is real. It just isn't coming from ethanol. The most common culprits are below.

## 8 Reasons You Might Feel Rough After Non-Alcoholic Beer

### 1. You stayed out late and slept badly

This is the big one, and it's easy to overlook. A night out on NA beer is still a night out. You went to bed later than usual, maybe in a loud or smoky place, maybe after a big meal. Then you probably drank several pints of liquid, which means a full bladder and one or two trips to the bathroom in the night.

Short or broken sleep alone produces headache, grogginess, low mood, and poor focus the next day. Those overlap heavily with hangover symptoms. If you'd like to understand how much of a normal hangover is really a sleep problem, our article on [whether sleep helps a hangover](/never-hungover/does-sleep-help-a-hangover) covers the evidence.

### 2. Carbonation and volume left you bloated

Four or five pints of anything fizzy is a lot of gas and liquid. Carbonation can cause bloating, burping, and an uncomfortable stomach, and a stretched stomach can make it harder to sleep comfortably. Some people also get mild reflux from beer-style drinks, alcoholic or not. The next morning, a sluggish, heavy feeling in your stomach can easily read as "hungover."

### 3. Sugar and carbohydrates

Many non-alcoholic beers have more sugar and carbohydrate than their regular versions. Brewers often stop fermentation early or remove alcohol after brewing, and they may add back body and sweetness to keep the flavor full. A few NA beers in an evening can add up to a meaningful amount of sugar, especially with salty bar snacks alongside.

For most people this just means a few extra calories. Some notice a heavy, sluggish feeling, thirst, or a dip in energy after a sugary evening. If you have diabetes or are watching your blood sugar, check the carbohydrate figure on the label. Brands vary widely, and some light or "low-carb" NA beers are much lower than others.

### 4. Histamine and other natural compounds in fermented drinks

Beer, wine, and other fermented drinks naturally contain small amounts of **histamine** and related compounds called biogenic amines, including **tyramine**. These come from the fermentation process, not from alcohol, so they can be present in non-alcoholic versions too, though levels vary a lot between products.

Most people break these down without noticing. People with **histamine intolerance** (a reduced ability to clear dietary histamine) may get a flushed face, stuffy nose, headache, itchy skin, or an upset stomach after fermented drinks, and they may notice it after NA beer or NA wine as well. Alcohol can make histamine reactions worse, so some people find NA drinks easier, but "less" isn't "none." Our guide to [histamine intolerance and alcohol](/never-hungover/histamine-intolerance-and-alcohol) explains the pattern.

Tyramine is the reason people taking **MAOI antidepressants** are often told to avoid tap or draft beer, including some non-alcoholic beers. In someone on an MAOI, a large tyramine load can trigger a dangerous spike in blood pressure with a severe headache. If you take an MAOI, ask your doctor or pharmacist which drinks, if any, are safe.

### 5. Gluten

Almost all non-alcoholic beer is made from barley, and many contain gluten. Removing alcohol doesn't remove gluten. If you have celiac disease or a gluten sensitivity, NA beer can cause bloating, gut pain, diarrhea, fatigue, and "brain fog" the next day, which can feel a lot like a hangover. Gluten-free NA beers do exist. Our [gluten-free alcohol guide](/never-hungover/gluten-free-alcohol) explains the difference between "gluten-free" and "gluten-reduced" labels, which applies to NA products too.

### 6. Hops, flavorings, and individual triggers

Some people get headaches from specific ingredients, and beer contains a lot of them: hops, malt, yeast residues, flavorings, and sometimes preservatives. If you get migraines, NA beer can still be a trigger for you, either because of its ingredients or because of the late night, irregular meals, and poor sleep that came with it. There's no good evidence that NA beer is a common migraine trigger on its own, but individual triggers are real, and a simple diary of what you drank and how you felt is the best way to find yours.

### 7. You expected to feel hungover

This one sounds dismissive, but it isn't. Expectations shape how we feel. Studies using placebo drinks (where people are told they are drinking alcohol but aren't) have found that some participants report feeling tipsy, and some report next-day symptoms. If your brain links "pints at the pub" with "rough morning," it can nudge you toward noticing every ache and yawn. That doesn't mean the symptoms are imaginary. It means the mind and body are connected, and the context of drinking can matter even without the alcohol.

### 8. You weren't actually drinking only NA beer

Worth double-checking. Did the bartender pour a regular pint once? Did you switch to a real drink later in the evening? Was one of the cans a craft "low-alcohol" beer (around 1% to 2.8%) rather than a true NA beer? Was the kombucha or "hard" seltzer stronger than you thought? Labels for low and no alcohol drinks can look similar at a glance, and small-batch fermented drinks such as kombucha can end up with more alcohol than expected. Our guide on [how much alcohol is in kombucha](/never-hungover/how-much-alcohol-is-in-kombucha) explains why.

Even then, one or two regular drinks among several NA beers is unlikely to produce a severe hangover. But it can explain a mild one.

## Can Non-Alcoholic Wine Give You a Hangover?

The same logic applies. Most non-alcoholic wine is made by producing regular wine and then removing the alcohol, usually down to 0.5% or less. That leaves very little ethanol, so a classic hangover is very unlikely.

But wine brings its own cast of non-alcohol suspects:

- **Sulfites.** These preservatives are often still present in non-alcoholic wine. Sulfites are a real problem for a small number of people, mainly those with sulfite sensitivity or certain kinds of asthma, who may get wheezing or flushing. For most people, though, sulfites are an unlikely cause of headache. Our article on [sulfites and wine headaches](/never-hungover/sulfites-in-wine-headaches) covers what the research does and doesn't support.
- **Histamine.** Red wines tend to contain more histamine than whites, and that doesn't disappear when the alcohol is removed. If red wine gives you a stuffy nose or flushed face even in small amounts, NA red might too.
- **Sugar.** Like NA beer, many NA wines contain more residual or added sugar than dry regular wine, so a few glasses can add up.
- **Tannins and polyphenols.** Some people report headaches from tannin-rich reds. The evidence here is limited, but individual sensitivity is possible.

An interesting wrinkle: a 2023 study from researchers at the University of California, Davis proposed that a flavonoid in red wine called quercetin may cause headaches by interfering with how the body processes alcohol, letting acetaldehyde build up. If that theory holds, the effect depends on alcohol being present, so it should matter much less with non-alcoholic red wine. The theory hasn't been confirmed in human trials yet. For more, see our guide to [red wine headaches](/never-hungover/red-wine-headache).

## What About Guinness 0.0 and Other Big-Brand NA Beers?

Guinness 0.0 is a good example because people often ask about it by name. According to Guinness, it's brewed like regular Guinness and then has the alcohol removed using cold filtration, and it's sold as an alcohol-free stout. Heineken 0.0, Athletic Brewing, Erdinger Alkoholfrei, Clausthaler, Budweiser Zero, and many others work on the same principle, using either removal after brewing or limited fermentation to keep alcohol very low.

Here's the honest assessment for big-brand NA beers:

**What's in their favor**

- Very low alcohol, often labeled 0.0% or under 0.5%, so no meaningful intoxication or classic hangover
- Consistent quality control from large brewers, which makes the stated alcohol level more reliable
- Usually fewer calories than regular beer
- They let you stay in a drinking social setting without the next-day cost of alcohol

**What to watch for**

- Most contain gluten unless labeled gluten-free
- Carbohydrate and sugar content can be higher than you'd guess, so check the label
- Fermented-drink compounds such as histamine and tyramine can still be present
- Drinking several pints of any fizzy drink late at night can disturb sleep and leave you bloated

A stout like Guinness 0.0 is not "heavier" on your system just because it's dark. The color comes from roasted barley, not from alcohol or more congeners. If you feel off after a few, look at the volume, the hour, and the food, not the color.

## NA Beer vs. Regular Beer: How the Morning After Compares

If you're weighing a switch, here's how the two compare on the things that drive a hangover:

| Factor | Regular beer (about 5%) | Non-alcoholic beer (0.0% to 0.5%) |
|---|---|---|
| Acetaldehyde from alcohol | Yes, scales with how much you drink | Negligible |
| Alcohol-driven fluid loss | Yes | Negligible, and the drink itself hydrates you |
| Alcohol-driven sleep disruption | Yes, worse in the second half of the night | No, though late nights and bathroom trips still count |
| Stomach irritation | Alcohol irritates the stomach lining | Carbonation and volume can still bloat |
| Congeners (flavor by-products of fermentation) | Low compared with dark spirits | Present in small amounts, but without alcohol they're not linked to hangovers |
| Gluten, histamine, sugar | Present | Present, sometimes more sugar |

The short version is that NA beer removes the parts of a hangover that come from alcohol and keeps the parts that come from the drink itself and the night around it. For most people, the first group is by far the bigger one. If you're curious about how fermentation by-products fit into the picture for regular drinks, our guide to [congeners in alcohol](/never-hungover/congeners-in-alcohol) and our article on the [beer hangover](/never-hungover/beer-hangover) go deeper.

## Does Non-Alcoholic Beer Dehydrate You?

No. Regular alcohol has a mild diuretic effect: it reduces a hormone called vasopressin that tells your kidneys to hold on to water, so you pass more urine than the fluid you drank would explain. At 0.5% or less, that effect essentially disappears. A non-alcoholic beer is mostly water, and it hydrates you about as well as other drinks do.

There's even a small amount of research looking at NA beer as a recovery drink for athletes, partly because some contain carbohydrates and polyphenols. The evidence is limited, and it doesn't make NA beer a sports drink, but it does show it isn't working against your hydration.

If you feel thirsty or dry-mouthed the next morning, salty food from the night before is a more likely cause. Our article on [whether alcohol dehydrates you](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-dehydrate-you) explains how much of the usual hangover is really about fluids.

## Alternating NA Beer With Regular Drinks: Does It Help?

Yes, and this may be the most useful way to use NA beer if you still drink. Swapping every other drink for an NA beer cuts the total alcohol you take in, slows your pace, and keeps a glass in your hand so you're less likely to be topped up. Fewer drinks means a lower peak blood alcohol and a milder morning.

A few honest caveats:

- The hangover you get will come from the regular drinks, not the NA ones. Two real beers and three NA beers will feel like two real beers, plus maybe some bloating.
- The NA beers don't "cancel out" the alcohol or speed up how fast your liver clears it.
- If you're using NA beer to cut back for a while, the [sober-curious guide](/never-hungover/sober-curious) has practical ideas for nights out.

For the habits with the best evidence for a better morning, see our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

## How to Feel Better the Morning After NA Beer

Because the cause isn't alcohol, the fix is mostly about the other factors.

1. **Drink some water and eat a proper breakfast.** This helps with any lingering sluggishness and steadies blood sugar after a sugary or salty evening.
2. **Get some sleep back if you can.** A short nap or an earlier night tonight will often do more than anything else.
3. **Ease the bloating.** A gentle walk helps move trapped gas. Skip more fizzy drinks for the day.
4. **Use a pain reliever only if you need one.** For a plain headache, a standard over-the-counter dose taken with food is reasonable for most adults. Follow the label, and ask a pharmacist if you have stomach, kidney, or liver problems or take other medicines.
5. **Keep a simple note.** If it happens more than once, write down the brand, how many you had, what you ate, and how you slept. Patterns usually show up fast, whether it's one brand with a lot of sugar, gluten, or a too-late night.

If you regularly feel unwell after small amounts of NA beer or wine, with flushing, hives, wheezing, or stomach symptoms, mention it to your doctor. Food intolerances, histamine intolerance, celiac disease, and sulfite sensitivity can all be checked for.

## Who Should Be Careful With Non-Alcoholic Beer

For most adults, NA beer is a sensible swap. But a few groups should check first, because "non-alcoholic" usually means *up to* 0.5% rather than zero, and fermented drinks carry other compounds too:

- **People taking disulfiram (Antabuse).** This drug causes a strong reaction to even small amounts of alcohol. Many doctors advise avoiding 0.5% products entirely.
- **People taking metronidazole** or certain other antibiotics and antifungals whose labels warn against alcohol. Ask your pharmacist whether trace alcohol matters for your prescription.
- **People taking MAOI antidepressants**, because of tyramine in some beers.
- **Pregnant people or those trying to conceive.** Major health bodies advise that no amount of alcohol is known to be safe in pregnancy, so many people choose 0.0% products or skip them. Talk it through with your doctor or midwife.
- **People with liver disease** or anyone told by a doctor to avoid all alcohol.
- **People who face alcohol testing** for work, court, or a medical program. Studies have shown that drinking large amounts of 0.5% beer can lead to positive results on very sensitive urine tests for alcohol by-products, even without any intoxication.
- **People with celiac disease**, unless the product is labeled gluten-free.

## A Quick Word on DHM

If you're reading this because you mix NA and regular drinks on a night out, it's natural to wonder about hangover supplements for the regular-drink part of the evening. **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the research is in animals and lab models, with limited human data, so it's promising rather than settled. There is no good evidence that DHM prevents hangovers in people, and it does nothing for the non-alcohol causes covered above, such as sugar, gluten, or a late night.

If you only drink 0.0% or 0.5% beer, you don't need a hangover supplement at all. If you do drink regular alcohol and want to try DHM, a popular budget option is [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20), and a higher-end blend is [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains timing and amounts, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. Drinking less and slower will always do more than any supplement.

## The Bottom Line

- Non-alcoholic beer at 0.5% or less contains too little alcohol to cause a true hangover. Your body clears it about as fast as you drink it.
- Feeling rough afterward is real, but the usual causes are a late night and poor sleep, carbonation and volume, sugar, histamine or gluten sensitivity, individual triggers, or expectations.
- Non-alcoholic wine and Guinness 0.0 work the same way: no meaningful alcohol, but sulfites, histamine, sugar, and gluten can still bother some people.
- If you mixed in regular drinks, the hangover comes from those.
- Check with a doctor before drinking NA beer if you take disulfiram, metronidazole, or an MAOI, are pregnant, have liver disease, or need to avoid alcohol completely.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can non-alcoholic beer give you a hangover?**

Not a true hangover. A 0.5% beer has about a tenth of the alcohol of a regular beer, and your body clears it about as fast as you drink it, so the alcohol-driven causes of a hangover never really get going. You can still feel rough the next day from a late night, poor sleep, bloating from carbonation, sugar, or a sensitivity to histamine or gluten.

**Why do I get a headache after non-alcoholic beer?**

The most common reasons are short or broken sleep, a late night in a loud or smoky place, not eating properly, and drinking a lot of fizzy liquid. Some people are sensitive to histamine, tyramine, gluten, or specific ingredients in beer, which can cause headaches without alcohol. If you get migraines, NA beer or the night around it can still be a trigger. A sudden, severe headache or one with fever, stiff neck, or confusion needs medical attention right away.

**Can non-alcoholic wine give you a hangover?**

Not in the classic sense, because dealcoholized wine usually contains 0.5% alcohol or less. But NA wine can still contain sulfites, histamine, tannins, and a fair amount of sugar, which can bother some people. If red wine gives you a stuffy nose or flushed face in small amounts, NA red might too.

**Can Guinness 0.0 give you a hangover?**

No more than any other 0.0% beer. Guinness says it removes the alcohol through cold filtration, leaving essentially none. Its dark color comes from roasted barley, not from extra alcohol. If you feel off after a few, the usual causes are volume, carbonation, gluten, and a late night.

**How many non-alcoholic beers would it take to get drunk?**

For practical purposes, you can't. At 0.5%, you'd need roughly ten 12 oz cans to match the alcohol in one regular beer, and your liver clears that alcohol about as fast as it arrives. You would be too full of liquid long before your blood alcohol rose to a level that causes intoxication.

**Does non-alcoholic beer dehydrate you?**

No. At 0.5% or less, the diuretic effect of alcohol is negligible, and NA beer is mostly water, so it hydrates you about as well as other drinks. Next-morning thirst is more likely from salty food or a late night.

**Can I drink non-alcoholic beer if I'm on medication?**

Often yes, but check first if your medicine carries an alcohol warning. People taking disulfiram, metronidazole, or MAOI antidepressants should talk to their doctor or pharmacist before drinking any NA beer, because trace alcohol or the tyramine in some beers can cause reactions. Pick a 0.0% product if you've been told to avoid all alcohol.

**Will drinking NA beer between regular drinks prevent a hangover?**

It can make the morning milder because you drink less alcohol overall and slow your pace. But it doesn't cancel out the alcohol you do drink or speed up how fast your body clears it. Any hangover you get will come from the regular drinks.
